questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might select an in-person handoff when you prefer the safety and convenience of a contactless delivery.

questions.question: How much should you tip the delivery person?
questions.why: The checkout screen presents several percentage-based tip options and a custom amount field, noting that tips are optional but go entirely to the driver.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means losing control over how much you financially reward the delivery driver based on your personal preferences and budget.

questions.question: What date of birth should I enter for the alcohol age verification?
questions.why: The screen requires a valid date of birth to verify you are 21 or older and warns that the recipient must present a driver's license or state ID in person.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent might enter a date of birth that does not match the physical ID you will need to show the delivery driver.

questions.question: Which phone number should you provide for order updates?
questions.why: The checkout screen requires a 10-digit mobile number so the service can text or call you about your order.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether to share their real personal number for driver communications or use a fake number to protect their privacy.

questions.question: Did I format my loyalty card number exactly as instructed before completing the purchase?
questions.why: The screen explicitly states the TOPS BonusPlus card must be 11 digits and start with a 4, which is required to successfully apply loyalty savings to the final total.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to earn rewards or receive store-specific discounts if the agent carelessly inputs an invalid loyalty card number.

questions.question: Which payment method do you want to use for this order?
questions.why: The checkout screen requires you to choose between your saved credit cards, adding a new card, or applying a gift card to pay the $46.14 total.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent might charge the groceries to a card you did not intend to use for this specific purchase.

questions.question: Have you entered the correct payment and billing details to finalize the checkout?
questions.why: The screen displays a payment form requiring card information and a billing address, which must be accurate to successfully process the charge.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over which specific payment method is charged and the privacy of entering your own sensitive financial details.

questions.question: Should you click 'Add Promo Code' to apply a discount to your order?
questions.why: The account menu displays an 'Add Promo Code' option that could be used to reduce the total cost of the groceries.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to save money by applying a promotional discount to their grocery bill.

questions.question: Are the final costs, including the service fee and tip, acceptable before placing the order?
questions.why: The order summary displays a final total of $315.10, which includes a $51.70 tip and a discounted service fee that must be verified before committing to the purchase.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the ability to adjust the tip amount or confirm that your membership discounts were properly applied to the final fees.

questions.question: Are the delivery details and order summary correct before adding a payment method?
questions.why: Verifying the address, delivery window, and order summary ensures the groceries will arrive at the right place and time before committing to the payment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to verify the final delivery instructions, time frame, and total cost before the purchase is finalized.

questions.question: Does the item count at checkout hold steady?
questions.why: The checkout screen showed the total item count drop from 14 to 12 and then back to 14, which could indicate a system glitch or missing items.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to catch a system error that might result in missing groceries or incorrect charges.

questions.question: Do the item prices in your cart match the prices shown when you added them?
questions.why: The Chex Mix is listed at $2.56 in the cart summary despite being priced at $2.55 when it was originally added to the cart.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to catch unexpected price changes or system glitches that increase the total cost of their order before paying.

questions.question: Did you actually place the order and see a confirmation screen?
questions.why: The narrator claims the order is placed, but the video cuts away from empty payment fields and a disabled 'Continue' button without ever showing a confirmation.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose visual proof that the checkout process was successfully completed and the grocery order was actually submitted.

children.label: Manage the live order
children.note: 8.1, then 8.2 as the interstitials land. the replacement triage is 6 re-entered item by item right after placing (rX1S, bpci, QeWn). 8.3 to 8.7 in whatever order the shopping run forces - 8.6 only when fulfillment itself fails (qpjw). 8.8 until the doorbell.

questions.question: What does the confirmation show?
questions.why: The 'You're all set!' message and the two-hour delivery window confirm that the transaction was successful and tell you when to expect your groceries.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate peace of mind of seeing the confirmation screen and knowing exactly when your groceries will arrive.

questions.question: Do you want to add any last-minute suggested items to your order?
questions.why: The screen displays a 'Need anything else?' prompt with featured deals and past purchases like Siggi's yogurt and Simply Lemonade, offering a final chance to add forgotten groceries.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to spot and add a forgotten staple or take advantage of a last-minute deal that an automated agent would likely skip.

questions.question: Do you want to purchase a gift card or skip this promotion to see your order status?
questions.why: The screen displayed a promotional page for Instacart gift cards with options to either send one or click 'Next' to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the opportunity to purchase a gift card for someone else before viewing your final order confirmation.

questions.question: A chat box to your shopper is open - do you want to word the request to add the forgotten item yourself?
questions.why: The screen displays a chat box to communicate with your shopper, allowing you to manually request last-minute additions to your order.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally and politely ask the human shopper for a favor using your own words.

questions.question: Which comb should you add to your existing order?
questions.why: The screen allows adding items to the confirmed order before shopping begins and displays several comb options ranging from $1.49 to $3.49.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to choose the specific brand, style, and price of the additional item being added to their final order.

questions.question: Do you want to review the specific items your shopper has already picked?
questions.why: The screen shows that your shopper, [name], has found 1 of your 14 items, and checking the list lets you monitor her progress and any substitutions.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally monitor the live shopping progress and intervene if an unwanted substitution is made.

questions.question: Did the item get added to your active order?
questions.why: Seeing the item count increase from 6 to 7 on the tracking screen confirms that your late addition was successfully included before the shopper started.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate reassurance of watching the order status and item count update to guarantee your late addition made it into the final order.

questions.question: Do you want the replacement the shopper is proposing, a different one, or a refund?
questions.why: The suggested replacement adds a $0.60 upcharge, but the alternatives shown are either much more expensive or completely different herbs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might blindly accept the price increase without checking the alternatives, or it might choose a cheaper but incorrect herb like chives.

questions.question: Has your order been reassigned to a new shopper?
questions.why: Checking the app for shopper updates reveals that a new shopper named [name] took over the order and shifted the delivery window to between 6:45 and 8:45.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose real-time awareness of who is handling your groceries and any unexpected delays to your delivery window.

questions.question: How do you want to acknowledge the shopper's final delivery update?
questions.why: The chat window displayed a message from the shopper confirming they would leave the order at the door, prompting a decision on whether to reply.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally express gratitude and build rapport with the person delivering your groceries.

questions.question: What is the current status of your order and its estimated delivery time?
questions.why: The screen displays an order progress bar and a map with a delivery ETA, allowing you to track when your groceries will arrive.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses real-time visibility into the delivery progress and the exact time they need to be available to receive the order.

questions.question: Does the confirmed delivery window match the initial estimate you selected?
questions.why: The final order status showing a 12:45pm-2:45pm window confirms that the initial 'Within 2 hours' estimate was honored.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to verify that the final delivery window actually aligns with the initial timeframe promised.

children.label: Verify the delivery
children.note: 9.1, then 9.2 to 9.4 in any order - only four keepers reach any of this on screen, and bpci alone sees a final receipt, for under a second.

questions.question: What does the completion notice say about the delivery?
questions.why: Checking the completion screen and the provided photo confirms that your groceries were successfully dropped off at your requested location.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the peace of mind of seeing the photographic proof of exactly where your groceries were left.

questions.question: Does the final confirmation screen show that your delivery instructions were followed?
questions.why: Checking that the completion screen confirms the order was left at the door with a photo ensures your specific delivery instructions were successfully applied.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the peace of mind of personally verifying that the delivery driver received and followed your specific drop-off instructions.

questions.question: Does the order page mention a temporary authorization above the total?
questions.why: Grocery delivery services often authorize a higher amount than the checkout total to account for potential substitutions or weighted items.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate awareness of how much money is temporarily held in your bank account, which could impact your available balance.

questions.question: What does the receipt's breakdown of final charges show?
questions.why: Checking the receipt screen ensures that the subtotal, taxes, tip, service fee, and discounts accurately match your expected total.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify exactly how their final fee structure was calculated and spot any unexpected charges.

questions.question: How should you rate and review the previous shopper's performance?
questions.why: The screen displays a prompt to rate a previous shopper with a five-star scale and feedback tags, which directly impacts the gig worker's future batch availability and income.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to exercise human empathy and provide a generous rating that protects the gig worker's livelihood.

healthinfo.task: look up specific health information online and judge its reliability (Mayo Clinic, WebMD, NIH/MedlinePlus, NHS): search a symptom, condition, or medication question, open results, distinguish reputable medical sources from ads and content farms, read the relevant section, and cross-check at least one second source; complete when the answer is on screen from an identified reputable source. Surface pinned: health-information websites reached through search. Variants: personal medical-record portals (that is a different task), telehealth appointment booking, health influencer/talking-head advice videos, and supplement marketing do not belong.

tree.label: Look up reliable health information
tree.note: do 1 - 1.4 and 1.5 only where a tool is gated (XwDq); the reference sites have no gate, and the same checker on the current site has none (1ch0). then 2, which picks 3 or 4 on a reference site or 5 on a checker; repeat 2 until a page answers - pQKZ drops the index for the search twice, FjnL drops a search for the index, y127 drops the index for the search. then 6, with 7 on the same page where the keeper does it. 8 for a second reading - FjnL runs 3 and 4 again on a second site, hIZP runs 1, 2 and 3 or 4 again on three more sites, kK4R runs 3 again, 1ch0 runs 5.2 again on the same pair, XwDq re-reads in 8.3. 8.5 loops back to 2 for the next topic - pQKZ four times - or to 5.2.5 for the next drug pair - 1ch0 three times.

children.label: Reach the health site
children.note: 1.1, 1.2 or 1.7 - every keeper arrives by address, by a library list, or by typing the site's name into Google (hIZP, three of its four sites); none types a symptom into a search engine. 1.3 whenever a banner sits on the entry page; 1.6 whenever a consent prompt, chat window or overlay covers the page - no keeper meets one. 1.4 then 1.5 only on the 2013 drugs.com (XwDq); the current drugs.com opens the same checker from a homepage tile with no registration and no terms page (1ch0). 1.5 alone where a form's Submit doubles as the terms (4Bl8).

children.label: Register an account
children.note: 1.4.1, with 1.4.2 and 1.4.3 as the form raises them, then 1.4.4; 1.4.5 when the site asks for verification after the fact. one keeper (XwDq), on the 2013 site; the reference sites never ask, and the current drugs.com runs the checker signed out (1ch0).

questions.question: The site wants an account with your age range before the tool runs. Should I create one?
questions.why: The screen shows a closed dropdown still displaying the 'Select Age' placeholder, indicating that an age range must be chosen to filter the health information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to provide their actual age, which is critical for receiving accurate and relevant medical information.

questions.question: Should you check the 'I am a Healthcare Professional' box?
questions.why: The screen presents an optional checkbox that, if selected, requires you to specify a job title and medical specialization.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to control the complexity of the medical content provided, as a professional profile might return highly technical clinical data instead of consumer-friendly explanations.

questions.question: Which newsletters or extras should be ticked when making the account?
questions.why: The registration form includes optional checkboxes for healthcare professionals and various email newsletters that determine the type and volume of emails you will receive.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over your email inbox preferences and the accuracy of your user profile if an agent makes these selections for you.

questions.question: Should I read the Terms & Conditions and Privacy Policy before agreeing to them?
questions.why: The screen requires checking a box to accept the site's terms and privacy policy, which dictate how your personal information will be handled.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to make an informed decision about whether they are comfortable with how the site collects and uses their sensitive health data.

questions.question: Does the site block the tool until the email is verified?
questions.why: The screen shows a membership verification warning that restricts forum posting, prompting a decision on whether completing account setup is necessary for your current task.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to decide whether to fully activate their account for community features or bypass the interruption to quickly access the health tool.

questions.question: Do you agree to the checker's own terms so it will open?
questions.why: The site presents a mandatory scrollable terms text box and an 'I Agree' button specifically for the Interactions Checker, separate from the account registration terms.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to read and consent to the tool's specific medical limitations and liability waivers before relying on its health information.

questions.question: Does the checker open after the terms are agreed to?
questions.why: The site displays a mandatory terms of service prompt that must be accepted before granting access to the interaction checker.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to review the specific terms and conditions you are accepting before entering your health information.

questions.question: On the cookie pop-up, do you want non-essential cookies rejected so your health query is not tracked?
questions.why: Health websites often use third-party trackers, and accepting all cookies can result in the user's sensitive medical condition being shared with data brokers and advertisers.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over their medical privacy, risking targeted advertising based on a sensitive health condition because the agent blindly clicked 'Accept All'.

questions.question: Is a chat bubble, pop-up, or banner covering the article?
questions.why: Health websites frequently use aggressive overlays that cover the main content, requiring the user to find and click a small 'X' to read the article.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user cannot see if the agent is reading text that is actually hidden behind an overlay, or if the agent accidentally clicked a deceptive ad while trying to close the pop-up.

children.label: Search for the site by name

questions.question: Is the result being opened the real site, rather than an ad or a lookalike?
questions.why: The search results display multiple links, making it important to verify that the URL is exactly 'https://www.webmd.com' to avoid clicking on deceptive ads or unreliable content farms.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally verify the search result URL to guarantee the information will come from an authentic, reputable medical source.

children.label: Choose the way in
children.note: 2.1 on any homepage, repeatedly when the keeper tours - y127 opens four sections before choosing one. then 2.2 picks 3, 4 or 5. 2.3 whenever a route lands wrong, and it sends the task back to 2.2 - pQKZ twice, FjnL once. 2.4 when the keeper opens a homepage feature instead of a way in - pQKZ six times, each closed with the back button, none leading to 3, 4 or 5. hIZP runs 2 once per site, four times, and gives a reason each time it picks the index or a section over the search bar.

questions.question: Should I open the Interactions Checker to look up the medicine?
questions.why: The screen shows the 'Your Account' overview page with the pointer hovering over the 'Interactions Checker' link, indicating a choice of which tool to use for the query.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to choose the specific tool or section of the health website they prefer to use for their research.

questions.question: Do you want the guided symptom checker, or a plain search for the condition?
questions.why: The WebMD homepage displays a dedicated 'WebMD symptomchecker' section with an orange 'Start Now' button to begin evaluating your health issue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether to use a guided symptom checker tool or simply search for your condition manually using a search bar.

questions.question: Does the body-system section that was opened actually list the condition?
questions.why: The narrator points out that using the body systems menu 'assumes that I know diabetes is a dysfunction of the endocrine system,' highlighting a prerequisite knowledge check for this navigation path.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the realization that a specific navigation path requires medical knowledge they might not have, which could lead an agent to guess or get stuck.

questions.question: Does the index have a general entry for the term, or only narrow ones?
questions.why: The alphabetical list displayed many specific magnesium compounds, indicating that a direct search might be better for finding a general overview.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to recognize when a site's directory is too granular and pivot to a more efficient search method.

questions.question: Does the site have a dedicated page for the topic, or only a passing mention?
questions.why: The text only mentions leprosy in passing while focusing broadly on general mycobacterial infections, indicating it might lack the specific depth you need.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the human judgment to quickly abandon a tangentially related article and pivot to a more focused search.

children.label: Search the topic
children.note: 3.1, then 3.2 when the box offers suggestions, then 3.3 and 3.4 on the results page. 3.4 goes back to 3.1 with a different term when the pick misses - pQKZ types the common name after the technical one failed in 4. hIZP runs 3 on three of its four sites with a partial name and takes the suggestion each time.

questions.question: Did the search actually run, or is the term still sitting in the box?
questions.why: The screen shows the MedlinePlus home page with the query typed in the search bar, indicating the search has not yet been executed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to review actual health information if the agent hallucinates being on a results page before actually submitting the search.

questions.question: What specific medical topic do you want to search for?
questions.why: Entering a precise topic into the MedlinePlus search box ensures the site retrieves the correct health information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the ability to choose the exact symptom or condition you want to investigate.

questions.question: Which suggested search term should you choose?
questions.why: The search dropdown shows both broad terms and specific subtopics like "diabetes medicines," which determines the scope of the medical information you will find.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether a broad overview or a specific subtopic best matches your actual health question.

questions.question: Did the search swap the term for a similar-sounding condition?
questions.why: Search engines often aggressively autocorrect complex drug names or medical conditions (e.g., changing 'hypothyroidism' to 'hyperthyroidism'), which completely changes the medical information returned.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to notice that the search results are for the wrong disease or medication entirely before clicking into them.

questions.question: Which kind of result should be opened, such as Health Topics or the encyclopedia?
questions.why: The search results page displayed thousands of links and specific refinement categories like 'Health Topics' and 'Medical Encyclopedia', making it important to choose the most direct path to a reliable overview.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to start with a broad summary overview or filter for specific formats like medical tests or external health links.

questions.question: Does the link chosen from the results lead to the full article on the reputable site, not an ad or a bare snippet?
questions.why: The search results display a brief summary of the condition, so you must identify the correct link to open the full article.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to verify that the chosen link leads to a comprehensive and reputable medical source instead of an ad or incomplete summary.

children.label: Browse the index
children.note: 4.1 then 4.3, or 4.2 in place of 4.1 where the site groups by body system. 4.3 lands on a page; when it is the wrong one, 2.3 takes over. pQKZ runs 4 three times and it works once; hIZP runs it once on MedlinePlus and the see-also row lands on the right page.

questions.question: When the index lists several entries for the term, which one matches what you asked?
questions.why: The screen displays a long list of health topics starting with 'D', requiring you to scroll past unrelated conditions like 'Dementia' and 'Depression' to find the exact match.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to see if the site breaks the condition down into more specific sub-categories, like Type 1 or Type 2, before clicking.

questions.question: Does the index entry send the term to a different name?
questions.why: The A-Z index lists terms like 'Halitosis' with a cross-reference to 'see Bad Breath', requiring you to click the redirected common name to find the information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to track how the medical site categorizes your specific symptom, which helps build your health literacy regarding clinical versus common terminology.

children.label: Query the interactive tool
children.note: 5.1 on a symptom checker, 5.2 on an interaction checker - the site decides which. 4Bl8 and XwDq run one check each; 1ch0 runs 5.2 four times, editing the list between runs. both end by handing a page to 6.

children.label: Describe the symptoms
children.note: 5.1.1, then 5.1.2 and 5.1.3, then 5.1.4 once per screen - nine screens for one symptom. 5.1.5 after the first list, which re-ranks it; then 5.1.6.

questions.question: What age and sex should go into the checker for the patient?
questions.why: The WebMD symptom checker requires the patient's age and gender to provide relevant results, while fields like zip code and email are optional.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might input incorrect patient demographics leading to irrelevant health information, or unnecessarily share your email address for marketing newsletters.

questions.question: Does the header above the checker show the age and sex that were entered?
questions.why: The screen displays a persistent header (e.g., 'Gender: Male', 'Age: 3-6 years') above the symptom body map, confirming the demographic filters currently applied to the tool.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to catch a silent error where the agent defaulted to an adult profile while researching a child's symptoms, which would lead to completely wrong medical triage.

questions.question: Which entry in the symptom list matches what you described?
questions.why: The screen shows a long alphabetical list of symptoms, making it essential to select the exact match to ensure the resulting medical information is relevant.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally translate your nuanced physical feelings into the most accurate clinical term provided by the tool.

questions.question: Did the symptom just picked show up in the 'Your Choices' list?
questions.why: The interface features a specific panel that tracks selected symptoms. If a click on the interactive body map or a checkbox fails to register, the symptom won't be added to this running list.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to verify that all their intended symptoms were actually captured by the tool before it calculates the possible conditions.

questions.question: The checker asks follow-up questions about the symptom. What are the answers, or should they be skipped?
questions.why: The screen offers a 'Skip Questions' button, but selecting specific options like 'about the same time of day' helps the tool narrow down the exact condition.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to provide nuanced personal details about the symptom's timing to get a highly tailored health assessment.

questions.question: Should you add more symptoms to narrow the possible conditions?
questions.why: The screen shows 49 possible conditions for a single headache symptom, which is too broad to pinpoint the actual health issue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to provide additional, specific symptoms about the patient that an agent wouldn't know but are necessary to filter the list accurately.

questions.question: Is the condition list being read the new one from after the extra symptoms went in, not the long one from before?
questions.why: The screen displays a narrowed list of three possible conditions alongside blue bars that visually indicate the probability of each ailment based on the symptoms entered.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to see how each additional symptom dynamically shifts the estimated probability of different underlying health conditions.

children.label: Check the drug list
children.note: 5.2.1 when the tool remembers an old list, then 5.2.2 once per drug - retyped when the box says No suggestions (1ch0). 5.2.3 only where the keeper is signed in (XwDq); 1ch0 runs every check on an Unsaved interactions list. then 5.2.4. for a follow-up question, 5.2.5 swaps one drug and returns to 5.2.4 - 1ch0 three times.

questions.question: Does the drug list still hold anything left over from an earlier check?
questions.why: The screen shows an unsaved drug list populated with previously entered medications that must be cleared using the 'New list' button to prevent them from interfering with the current search.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the assurance that the agent will correctly clear out old, irrelevant data before beginning a new health inquiry.

questions.question: After the drug is picked from the dropdown, does it actually show up in the list, or does the list still say it is empty?
questions.why: The screen shows an empty drug name field and states your interactions list is empty, indicating that a medication must be successfully selected to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to verify that the exact medication and formulation you are taking is correctly entered into the safety checker.

questions.question: When the dropdown offers several versions of the drug, which one matches what you take?
questions.why: The search field suggests several different brands, dosages, and combination medications like Aspir 81 and Aspir-Mox, requiring a specific selection.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify the exact formulation or brand of the medication that matches your personal health inquiry.

questions.question: Should the drug list be saved to the account?
questions.why: The modal offers the choice to customize the list name and save it either as a basic list or a more detailed Mednotes profile.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to organize their saved drug interactions using a custom name or an integrated health profile.

questions.question: Does the list show exactly the drugs asked about, before the check runs?
questions.why: The screen showed a specific list of four medications, including Amoxil and Cymbalta, queued up for an interaction check.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to verify that their exact medication list is complete and accurate before generating the interaction report.

children.label: Edit the list for the next pair
Read the answer page
children.note: 6.1 first on every page that has one; 6.2 where the page is long; 6.3 on the encyclopedia. then 6.4, and 6.5 where the page carries them - y127 scrolls past both red boxes, hIZP reads three of them aloud. 6.6 moves to a neighbouring page and back into 6; 6.7 is reached on two pages and taken on neither. on the interaction report 6.1 is the severity tally and 6.4 is the paragraph under the badge - 1ch0 reads MANAGEMENT on the second report after skipping it on the first.

questions.question: What does the report say about this pair?
questions.why: The screen displays a section with red exclamation marks labeled 'MAJOR' for specific drug pairs, highlighting critical safety warnings that require immediate attention.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally evaluate the specific risks and warnings associated with combining your exact medications.

questions.question: Which section of the page answers what was asked?
questions.why: The screen displays multiple detailed sections like 'Symptoms', 'Treatment', and 'When to See Your Doctor', requiring you to locate the exact information you need.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally absorb the nuances of the symptoms and self-care advice that might be uniquely relevant to your situation.

questions.question: What does the page say needs urgent medical help right away?
questions.why: The screen explicitly lists severe symptoms like bloody stools and fever that require immediate medical intervention rather than just being common, mild reactions.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the personal awareness of exactly which severe symptoms to watch out for in your own body.

questions.question: Did the symptom checker trigger a 'seek emergency care immediately' red flag that halts the questionnaire?
questions.why: Entering severe symptoms like chest pain or sudden weakness often causes triage tools to lock the interface and instruct the user to call 911 rather than providing informational conditions.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the critical triage context that their symptoms represent a medical emergency requiring immediate real-world action, not just further online reading.

children.label: Judge the source
children.note: 7.5 before 1 where the narrator names the sites in advance - hIZP and 1ch0. 7.1 to 7.3 on the page in hand, in any order and rarely more than one - pQKZ reads the date, kK4R reads the providers, y127 speaks the disclaimer; hIZP and 1ch0 read neither a date nor an author on five sites. 7.4 belongs before 3.4 on any search-engine entry with a symptom as the query and never happens in this corpus.

questions.question: How recently was this medical information reviewed or updated?
questions.why: Checking the review date in the article footer ensures the health advice is current and reflects the latest medical guidelines.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the personal reassurance of seeing exactly when the medical information was last vetted by professionals.

questions.question: Who does the page credit for writing, reviewing, and funding it?
questions.why: The page footer explicitly lists the organizations involved in development, production, and funding, such as the Santa Clara County Library and National Network of Libraries of Medicine.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally evaluate the financial and institutional backing of the health information to judge its independence and reliability.

questions.question: Who provides the links in the Start Here section?
questions.why: The screen showed a 'Start Here' section with links to introductory materials from reputable organizations like the American Academy of Family Physicians.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide which specific introductory resources or providing organizations they trust most to begin their research.

questions.question: Does the site carry ads?
questions.why: The narrator highlights that MedlinePlus is recommended specifically 'because the site has no advertising and its information is reviewed by experts,' making ad-presence a key heuristic for reliability.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to use the presence of advertising as a personal heuristic for judging the commercial bias and reliability of a medical source.

questions.question: Is the top of the search results an ad or an AI summary rather than a medical site?
questions.why: Searches for specific drugs often trigger ads from law firms seeking plaintiffs for side-effect lawsuits, or ads for alternative medicine, which can look like legitimate health information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to spot the 'Sponsored' tag and avoid biased or alarmist content designed to sell a service rather than inform.

questions.question: Which website should you open to check for drug interactions?
questions.why: Choosing the right website matters because you need a dedicated, reliable tool like Drugs.com to accurately check interactions between Warfarin and Aspirin as instructed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to select your preferred or most trusted medical database for evaluating specific medication interactions.

questions.question: Is the page open on one of the reputable medical sites, not a general or crowd-written one?
questions.why: The task explicitly requires using authoritative medical sources like the Mayo Clinic or NIH, whereas the screen shows a search for the crowdsourced site Wikipedia.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the guarantee of medical accuracy if the agent cross-checks health information using a user-edited encyclopedia instead of a verified medical institution.

children.label: Cross-check the answer
children.note: 8.1 or 8.2 or 8.3 as a second reading - two keepers each, and three keepers take none. hIZP is all 8.1: the same question on four sites, never compared. 1ch0 takes 8.3 as its first reading on every report and 8.2 once, to confirm a badge. 8.4 is offered on two sites and taken on neither; the one kept answer is typed onto a slide (1ch0). 8.5 closes every page and returns to 2 - pQKZ seven times - or to 5.2.5 for the next drug pair.

questions.question: Does the answer rest on one page, or has a second reputable site been read too?
questions.why: The screen shows the user opening a new tab to navigate to MedlinePlus after reviewing the first source.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that the health information has been properly cross-checked against a second reputable source.

questions.question: Does the drug information you found on this second site match what you read on the first?
questions.why: Comparing the facts between the two sources confirms whether the medical information is consistent and safe to trust.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally evaluate any subtle differences or contradictions in the medical advice provided by different sources.

questions.question: Do you want the consumer version or the professional one?
questions.why: The screen provides explicit options to switch between consumer and professional interaction data, which determines the complexity and depth of the medical information displayed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to choose the level of medical detail that best matches your personal health literacy and specific informational needs.

questions.question: Should the report be saved or sent anywhere?
questions.why: The results page displays Email, Print, and Save options that let you keep an accurate record of the drug list to discuss with a medical professional.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose the most convenient format, such as a physical printout, for sharing these specific health findings with your doctor.

questions.question: Is the quoted interaction for exactly the pair asked about, not another pair on the report?
questions.why: The slide asks if Allopurinol is a good choice for a patient taking Captopril, making it crucial to confirm that the website's 'Major' interaction warning directly addresses this exact combination.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the certainty that the final medical conclusion accurately reflects the specific patient scenario you originally needed to evaluate.

healthinsurance.task: shop for or enroll in a health insurance plan online (healthcare.gov, a state exchange, an employer open-enrollment portal, the Medicare plan finder): enter household and income details where asked, compare plans on premium, deductible, and network, select a plan and proceed toward enrollment; complete when the enrollment confirmation or the plan-selection summary is on screen. Surface pinned: the marketplace or enrollment flow — not insurance-explainer talking heads (that is policyinfo-class content).

tree.label: Get health insurance coverage
tree.note: do 1, with 2 where the venue shows rules and windows - three keepers land straight in the forms and skip 2. then 3, and 4 where drug costs drive the choice (the four Medicare keepers). the middle by regime: 5 on the marketplace routes, 6 on the employer routes, neither on the entitlement route - the benefit is fixed and the work is proving eligibility (iPQr, BEkw). 5 reaches back into 4 and re-reads the list until the configuration settles (fB0o, 5ISG, ma8-). then 7 where an application exists - on the employer routes the elections are the application, so 6 goes straight to 8. then 8, and 9 as far as the venue lets verification run in-session.

questions.question: Do you want to learn more about your options first, or are you ready to view plans?
questions.why: The site asks if you want to learn more about Medicare options or view plans directly to determine if you need educational guidance before shopping.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent decides whether to skip the educational materials, potentially bypassing foundational information you might have wanted to review.

children.label: Reach the enrollment system
children.note: 1.1, then whichever entry the venue demands: 1.2 with 1.3 where the portal re-asks inside (mtI4), 1.4 where the login fails or the site allows it (Lwux, all four Medicare keepers), 1.5 on the captcha-only portal, 1.6 when an agent works someone else's case. then 1.7 where enrollment lives behind an event or a banner.

questions.question: Will you log in to your account or proceed as a guest to start comparing plans?
questions.why: The homepage provides options to "Find health & drug plans" directly or "Log in" to access your personal information and saved preferences.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step requires sharing your secure Medicare account credentials with an agent.

questions.question: Do you need to create a new account to proceed?
questions.why: The login screen provides a "Create an account" button for users who do not yet have a secure Medicare account to save their information and compare plan costs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent will establish your secure Medicare account credentials on your behalf, which requires sharing highly sensitive personal information.

questions.question: Which search result is the official Medicare.gov link, and which are ads or third-party sites?
questions.why: The search results displayed several commercial ads and third-party sites before the official Medicare.gov link.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to verify they are using the official government portal instead of a commercial broker's site.

questions.question: Is my username entered correctly to proceed to the password step?
questions.why: The screen shows a login page with a username field and a 'Continue' button, which must be correct to access the application.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to verify that the correct account is being accessed before proceeding.

questions.question: Can you log in? The page needs your username and password.
questions.why: The login screen requires a username and password to access the enrollment portal and offers a checkbox to save the username for future visits.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means handing over your private account credentials and losing direct control over whether they are stored on the device.

questions.question: What is the one-time password sent to your mobile number?
questions.why: The portal requires the OTP sent to your phone to verify your identity before you can proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means sharing a time-sensitive security code, which compromises your account's multi-factor authentication protections.

questions.question: Do you want to review and update the application that was started for you?
questions.why: The screen shows that a pre-filled application is available and outlines the steps and deadline to complete it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to decide whether to proceed with the pre-filled application or start a new one.

questions.question: Are you ready to start the process to renew or change your coverage?
questions.why: The portal requires you to complete all enrollment steps to secure coverage for the upcoming year, even if you just want to keep your current plan.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You miss seeing the exact deadlines for when you need to enroll to get specific coverage start dates.

children.label: Learn the rules and window
children.note: any of it, in any order, before the choices open - 2.4 is the one hard gate (mtI4). the marketplace keepers mostly skip this goal; the welfare keepers read 2.3 and 2.5 as static pages before applying.

questions.question: What is my default plan for next year if I don't make a change?
questions.why: The screen displays the specific 2026 plan you will default into, which is critical to identify because its premiums and benefits may change from your current coverage.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the direct awareness of which plan you will automatically roll over into and the reminder that its costs and coverage might change next year.

questions.question: Do you meet the specific disability eligibility criteria for the Niramaya scheme?
questions.why: The presentation explicitly lists Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation, and Multiple Disabilities as the covered conditions, so you must confirm your eligibility before proceeding to the portal.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might blindly navigate to the enrollment portal without verifying if your specific condition qualifies under these strict guidelines.

questions.question: Do you have the required UDID card and understand that this scheme is reimbursement-only?
questions.why: The scheme description explicitly states that coverage requires a valid disability certificate or UDID card and operates strictly on a reimbursement basis.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might enroll you in a plan you are ineligible for or commit you to upfront out-of-pocket costs you cannot afford.

questions.question: What are the rules and requirements for creating my account?
questions.why: The screen displayed a warning popup with seven specific instructions in Bengali that outline the requirements for proceeding.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to know the specific rules and obligations you are agreeing to when setting up your health insurance account.

questions.question: Do you accept the warning that your information cannot be edited after submission?
questions.why: The screen displays a notice stating that edits won't be possible after submission, requiring you to click 'I Understand & Accept' to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to personally acknowledge the strict no-edit policy before proceeding with the application.

questions.question: What steps are required to complete the online registration process?
questions.why: The screen outlines a six-step process for online registration, including document uploads and payment, which sets expectations before starting the application.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you miss the upfront overview of the specific documents and steps required to successfully apply.

questions.question: Do you want to read the salient features of the scheme?
questions.why: The 'Home' dropdown contains links to 'Eligibility' and 'Salient Features', which explain the key benefits of the program before you start the application.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user misses the chance to read the program's highlights and confirm it aligns with their expectations.

children.label: Describe who needs covering
children.note: the venue's intake in its own order - 3.1 first on the agent route, where the answers exist on paper before the site is touched. 3.2 to 3.7 as asked; 3.8 where the form ends in a screening verdict (Lwux).

questions.question: What ZIP code and which kind of Medicare plan should I search for?
questions.why: The system needs your coverage year, ZIP code, and specific plan type—such as a Part D drug plan—to display the correct Medicare options for your area.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure the search is tailored to your specific location, timeline, and exact Medicare coverage needs.

questions.question: How should you answer the questions about your current Medicare coverage and drug assistance?
questions.why: The screen asks for your current Medicare coverage type and whether you receive help paying for prescription drugs to tailor the plan results.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to provide their exact current coverage and assistance details, which affects the accuracy of the plan recommendations.

questions.question: Should you switch from viewing standalone drug plans to viewing Medicare Advantage plans?
questions.why: The search results page currently displays standalone drug plans but offers a link at the top right to view available Medicare Advantage plans instead.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might select a comprehensive Medicare Advantage plan when you only wanted standalone prescription drug coverage, or vice versa.

questions.question: Do the coverage year and ZIP on the page match what you gave me?
questions.why: Choosing the right coverage year and ZIP code ensures you are viewing the correct health plans and prices available for your specific location and timeframe.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the ability to personally verify that the search is targeting your exact local market for the upcoming year.

questions.question: What pincode and mobile number should you enter to view the available plans?
questions.why: The screen requires a valid pincode and mobile number before the 'VIEW PLANS' button can be used to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent might enter an incorrect location or phone number, leading to inaccurate plan options or misdirected communications.

questions.question: Are my dependents listed correctly, or do I need to add anyone else?
questions.why: The screen lists your spouse and child with their details, and you must confirm this is accurate or use the 'add dependent +' link to ensure everyone who needs coverage is included.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting an agent handle this means you lose the chance to personally verify that your family members' sensitive details, like SSNs and dates of birth, are entered correctly.

questions.question: Who needs coverage and how old are they?
questions.why: Selecting the specific family members from the dropdown and entering their ages determines the exact coverage needs and pricing for your household.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure the agent accurately inputs your household composition and ages, which directly dictates your plan options and costs.

questions.question: Is your pre-filled personal information accurate and up to date?
questions.why: Verifying your pre-filled name, date of birth, and address ensures your insurance application is processed correctly.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to catch and correct outdated personal details like your address or tobacco use status before they are submitted.

questions.question: Do you want to check if your household can save money on coverage costs?
questions.why: The application overview highlights that determining eligibility for financial assistance is a primary goal of the form.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to explicitly choose whether to pursue the cost-savings evaluation path before beginning the application.

questions.question: Is this calculated monthly income right?
questions.why: The screen shows a calculated monthly income of $0.00 from your self-employment and asks if this estimate is correct or if your income is hard to predict.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to correct the system's zero-dollar estimate and accurately report your unpredictable self-employment income.

questions.question: Do you qualify for any financial assistance with your drug costs?
questions.why: The screen displays your Extra Help status for the upcoming years, indicating whether your income qualifies you for assistance with Medicare costs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you miss seeing your official eligibility status for financial assistance, which could drastically change how you budget for your prescriptions.

questions.question: How much of a premium tax credit do you qualify for?
questions.why: The screen displays your eligibility results and a specific tax credit amount, which directly determines your actual out-of-pocket costs when comparing plans.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally verify your exact financial assistance amount and understand how it will offset your monthly premiums.

children.label: Enter the drugs and pharmacies
children.note: runs only where drug costs drive the choice - the intake's own question opens it (4.1). 4.2 and 4.3 per drug, 4.4 where the system knows a generic, 4.5 closes each pass; repeat until the list is done. 4.7 for up to five slots. 4.6 and 4.8 are the re-entry points - 5's plan reaches back here because the estimate is conditional on this goal's outputs.

questions.question: Which prescription drugs, dosages, and refill frequencies should you add to your list?
questions.why: Entering your specific medications, exact dosages, and refill frequencies ensures the system can accurately estimate out-of-pocket costs and check plan formularies.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the assurance that your exact medications and dosages are correctly entered to find a plan that covers your specific health needs.

questions.question: Do you want to include your prescription drug costs in the plan comparison?
questions.why: The screen asks if you want to see your drug costs when comparing plans, which determines whether the system will calculate out-of-pocket expenses for your specific medications.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent might skip entering your medications, potentially resulting in a plan choice that does not adequately cover your specific prescriptions.

questions.question: Which of your recently filled medications do you want to add to your plan comparison list?
questions.why: The screen presented a list of recently filled drugs to include for cost estimates, and selecting the right ones ensures accurate plan comparisons.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent would not know which of your past medications you still take or want to factor into your future plan's cost estimates.

questions.question: Do the prepopulated dosage and quantity match your current prescription?
questions.why: Adjusting the dosage and quantity fields for your medication ensures the system calculates accurate out-of-pocket costs for your specific prescription needs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might accept the default medication values, leading to inaccurate cost estimates that do not reflect your actual prescription usage.

questions.question: Do you want to add the generic version of this drug to potentially save money, or keep the brand name?
questions.why: The portal offers a generic alternative that might cost less, which directly impacts the estimated out-of-pocket costs used to compare plans.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might automatically select the cheaper generic option, overriding your specific medical need or preference for the brand-name medication.

questions.question: What location and pharmacy name should I use to find pharmacies you like?
questions.why: The screen allows you to search for up to five pharmacies by zip code and name to ensure the plans you compare cover your preferred locations.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to ensure the plans being compared include the specific pharmacy locations that are most convenient for you.

questions.question: Which specific pharmacy location do you want to add to your profile?
questions.why: The search results display multiple CVS locations near [number], such as the ones on Whitmore Lake Rd and Challis Rd, so you must select the exact one you visit to ensure accurate prescription pricing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify your preferred local pharmacy, which could result in the agent selecting a location that is less convenient for you to visit.

questions.question: Do you want to check if other local pharmacies offer lower estimated drug costs?
questions.why: The screen shows a significant difference between your current retail pharmacies and the preferred mail-order option, making it worth checking if other local pharmacies offer better rates.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to optimize your out-of-pocket costs by comparing prices across your preferred local pharmacies.

questions.question: Which pharmacies do you currently have saved on your profile?
questions.why: The screen displays your saved pharmacies, which helps determine if your preferred locations are in-network for the plans you are comparing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might not know which specific local or mail-order pharmacies you prefer to use, potentially leading to the selection of a plan with poor coverage for your locations.

children.label: Compare the plans
children.note: 5.1 where filters exist - 5.1 also owns the empty-set escape (Lwux). 5.2, then 5.3 on the ranked cards; 5.4 per candidate, and most keepers walk exactly one. the loop the corpus insists on: reach back into 4.6 or 4.8, change an input, and re-read 5.3 - the ranking is not stable under the inputs (fB0o, 5ISG, ma8-).

questions.question: How do your new medications affect your current plan's estimated costs and coverage?
questions.why: Confirming that your current plan covers all four drugs for an estimated $30.00 provides a clear baseline before you search for alternative plans.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the direct reassurance of seeing exactly how your specific prescriptions impact your out-of-pocket costs under your current coverage.

questions.question: What minimum star rating do you want to require for the plans?
questions.why: Filtering by star rating narrows down the 27 available prescription drug plans to only those meeting your specific quality standards.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide how strictly to weigh quality ratings against having a wider variety of plans to choose from.

questions.question: Do you want to filter for plans that are accepted across the U.S.?
questions.why: Checking the "Accepted across U.S." box narrows the available options down to 18 prescription drug plans that offer national coverage.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether having nationwide pharmacy access is more important than seeing the full, unfiltered list of local plan options.

questions.question: How do you want to sort the available prescription drug plans to compare your options?

itinerary.task: research and assemble travel options for a specific trip using travel-planning tools (Google Flights, Google Travel/Maps, Skyscanner, Kayak, Rome2Rio): search flights for dates, compare times, prices, and stops, check hotels or things-to-do for the same dates, and gather a shortlist of concrete options with prices — the person makes the final call, so booking is NOT required; complete when a compared set of options (e.g. a flights list filtered/sorted, tracked prices, or a saved shortlist) is on screen. Surface pinned: travel-search and planning tools in a browser or app. Variants: destination vlogs/guides ("top 10 things in Rome"), booking-only videos with no comparison (the hotel and flights domains cover booking), and travel-hacking/points content do not belong.
