questions.why: The form requires your previous ZIP code, city, state, and street address, including any apartment or PO Box numbers, to correctly identify the mail to forward.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure your previous address details are formatted exactly as the post office recognizes them.

questions.question: Does the old address you entered match the business's officially registered address?
questions.why: The USPS form shows '[address]' as the old address, but the Idaho Secretary of State registry displays different street numbers for the business.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that their business mail will be properly forwarded if an incorrect old address is submitted.

questions.question: What is your new address?
questions.why: The screen requires your new street address, city, state, and ZIP code to determine exactly where your forwarded mail should go.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the chance to personally verify that your new address and any apartment numbers are entered without typos.

questions.question: Did the ZIP Code actually autofill when you selected the street address from the dropdown?
questions.why: The narrator claimed the ZIP Code would autofill, but the screen showed the field remaining as '[number]' for both the old and new addresses.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that their mail will be forwarded to the correct location if the agent fails to notice and correct the broken ZIP Code autofill.

questions.question: Should you opt into the free Informed Delivery service?
questions.why: The screen offers an optional checkbox to sign up for a free service that lets you digitally preview incoming mail and track packages at your new address.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether you want the convenience of digital mail previews or prefer to avoid additional email notifications.

questions.question: Do you want to expand and read the full Privacy Act Statement before clicking next?
questions.why: The screen displays a partial privacy statement noting your data will be used for mail forwarding, fraud mitigation, and advertisements, but the full text requires clicking to expand.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to fully understand the legal details of how your personal information will be used and shared by the USPS.

questions.question: Are you OK with your information also being used for move-related ads?
questions.why: The screen displays a Privacy Act Statement explaining that your data will be used for move-related advertisements, identity verification, and fraud mitigation.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally review and consent to the specific ways the USPS will use your personal information.

questions.question: When the form rejects an invalid field and returns to the top of Step 1, does it keep your other entries or discard them?
questions.why: The screen returned to the top of Step 1 because the form requires valid data, such as a correct state and ZIP code, to proceed to the next step.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the choice of whether to provide real personal information to complete the form or to stop the process.

questions.question: Are all the required fields on this step filled in before clicking Next?
questions.why: Leaving required fields blank triggers validation errors and prevents you from advancing to the move date selection screen.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to personally verify that their specific contact and move details are entered accurately before proceeding.

questions.question: Is the move information, including your old and new addresses, correct as shown?
questions.why: The screen displays a summary of the entered move details, which must be accurate to ensure mail is forwarded correctly.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify their personal move details before proceeding to payment and submission.

questions.question: Do you want to opt into the MYMOVE promotional offers shown on the standardization review screen?
questions.why: The USPS standardizes your address and removes special characters from your name, so you must verify the changes and decide whether to receive promotional offers.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to correct any errors introduced by the address standardization process and to decide whether to receive promotional moving offers.

children.label: Verify identity and pay
children.note: 4.1, then 4.2 where offered, then 4.3 then 4.4; a billing address different from both move addresses means going back to 2.6 - the rule pushes the start date at least seven days out

questions.question: Did the forwarding start date change after a different billing address was entered?
questions.why: Entering a separate billing address triggered a system rule that forced the forwarding start date to be at least seven days in the future.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to evaluate if the delayed start date is acceptable or if they need to adjust their billing method to keep their original date.

questions.question: Which of these addresses is your card's actual billing address?
questions.why: The screen requires you to select whether your credit card billing address matches your old address, new address, or a different address to successfully verify your identity.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify the correct billing address for your credit card, which could cause the identity verification process to fail.

questions.question: Does the free period's end date land exactly 12 months after your start date?
questions.why: Checking that the end date is exactly 12 months after the start date ensures the system correctly registered the full forwarding period.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify that their mail will be forwarded for the correct duration without any system errors.

questions.question: Do you want to purchase extended mail forwarding beyond the included 12 months?
questions.why: The screen offers an optional, nonrefundable purchase to extend mail forwarding beyond the standard free year.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide if they want to pay extra for a longer mail forwarding period.

questions.question: Which credit or debit card will you use to pay the identity-verification fee?
questions.why: The USPS requires a $1.05 charge to a valid credit or debit card whose billing address matches your selected address to verify your identity.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to keep your sensitive credit card details and billing information private from the agent.

questions.question: Does the page show the identity-verification payment as completed?
questions.why: The site explicitly states a $1.10 charge is required for the service, but the recording ends before any payment is made.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the certainty that their change-of-address request was successfully submitted since the mandatory payment was skipped.

questions.question: Does the final checkout total match the identity-verification fee stated at the beginning of the process?
questions.why: Checking that the fee in the order summary matches the initially stated $1.10 ensures you are paying the correct official USPS charge without hidden fees.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally verify the transaction amount before your payment method is charged.

children.label: Submit and keep the proof
children.note: 5.1 then 5.2; 5.3 for every registration the site itself warns it will not update

questions.question: Does the offers page's wording make it sound like the change of address is already done when it isn't yet?
questions.why: The page states both 'as a thank you for completing your Change-of-Address' and 'Before confirming your information', creating confusion about whether the process is finished.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally verify if their change-of-address application has actually been completed or still requires confirmation.

questions.question: Do you want to select any of the promotional offers from partner brands before continuing?
questions.why: The screen presents optional exclusive savings and coupons from various brands that can be emailed to you before you confirm your information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to choose which, if any, promotional discounts you want to receive or to explicitly opt out to avoid unwanted marketing emails.

questions.question: Does the page show the change-of-address confirmation screen with a confirmation code or confirmation-email notice?
questions.why: The video ends before the final submission step, meaning there is no confirmation code or email notice shown on screen to prove the process was completed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the certainty that your mail forwarding request was successfully submitted and processed by the USPS.

questions.question: Do you want to update your voter registration now that your change of address is complete?
questions.why: The final confirmation screen includes an optional prompt and link to update your voter registration for your new address.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to conveniently update your voter registration immediately after changing your mailing address.

questions.question: Does the USPS page warn that this change of address does not automatically update other agencies, such as the state, IRS, or voter rolls?
questions.why: The USPS site explicitly warns that submitting a change of address does not automatically update government agencies.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You miss the critical warning that you must separately update your state business registration to remain compliant.

children.label: File at a post office instead
children.note: 6.1 then 6.2 then 6.3; 6.4 is the counter alternative to the whole online form

questions.question: Do you want to complete the change of address online or in person using a paper form?
questions.why: The screen displays the official paper PS Form 3575, highlighting that you have the option to bypass the online process by visiting a post office.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to choose the in-person paper form alternative, which avoids the online identity verification fee.

questions.question: What location and search radius should you use to find a nearby post office?
questions.why: The form requires a city, state, or ZIP code along with a search radius to locate a post office.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose the most convenient search area and location for your in-person visit.

questions.question: Do you want to review the operating hours and services for this specific post office?
questions.why: The screen displayed the retail, lobby, and collection hours for the Downtown Blacksburg Post Office, which is necessary information if your identity verification requires an in-person visit.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally verify the post office's schedule to plan a convenient time for their visit.

videocall.task: set up or join a video call (Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams): either create/schedule a meeting and invite someone, or join with a link or code; work through the audio/video device prompts and arrive in the live meeting; complete when the in-meeting screen with the user's own audio/video controls is shown. Surface pinned: the meeting product's own host/join flow — not webinar spectating, not call-quality reviews, not presentations ABOUT video calling.

tree.label: Join a video call
tree.note: 1 where the session is not already inside the product - most keepers start signed in; 1.6 on the four Zoom sign-ups. then either the host route or the guest route. host: 2 for a meeting now or a link for later, or 3 for a scheduled one, then 4 to get the joining information out - 4 can also run from inside the meeting after 5. guest: 5.1 to 5.7 to find the way in. both routes run 5.8 where the product asks about opening the app, then 5.10 and 5.11; a guest may stop in 5.12. 6 on the host side once a guest asks to join. 7 and 8 in any order while the meeting runs - every keeper that reaches 5.11 tours them. 9 to leave, and 9.4 loops back to 5.

children.label: Get into the meeting product
children.note: 1.1 on every keeper that does not start inside the product. 1.2 once, where Meet is missing from Gmail. 1.3 where a sign-in is shown; 1.4 before joining where the narrator bothers; 1.5 where the account's right to host is in doubt. 1.6 in place of 1.3 on the four Zoom sign-ups. 1.7 where no client is installed - 6fIY enters it from 5.8 mid-join. 1.8 where the tutorial changes the name others will see - 0Qvm after the call, PQBe before scheduling.

children.label: Create the account
children.note: 1.6.1 first on every Zoom sign-up - four keepers read the plans and all four pick free. then 1.6.2; 1.6.3 on the two that meet an age check; 1.6.4 only on the email route (PQBe), never on the Google route (JlRf, QOUw). then 1.6.5, 1.6.6 and 1.6.7 in the order Zoom presents them - 1h5z starts this goal and a cut skips the rest.

questions.question: What name do you want others to see in the meeting?
questions.why: The 'Personal info' page shows your current name is set to '[name] Lessons' and notes that anyone can see this information when communicating with you.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to present themselves with a preferred professional or personal name to other meeting participants.

children.label: Create the meeting
children.note: 2.1 on every host that does not schedule - the choice is made in that menu. then 2.2 or 2.3. 2.4 only in the nickname era and on the Messenger room. 2.5 where the start dialog offers toggles - 1h5z reads them and starts anyway. 1h5z cancels 2.2 on its spinner and goes to 3 instead. from here to 4 or straight to 5.10.

children.label: Schedule the meeting
children.note: 3.1 opens the form - on Google Meet it is always a Calendar event and the homepage only hands off. then 3.2 to 3.6 in the form's order, skipping what the tool does not show; 3.6 is the whole reason for the Calendar route. 3.7 and 3.8 on Zoom, where half the form is security and entry defaults. 3.10 wherever a guests field exists - most keepers skip it and say they will share the link instead; 3.11 on the two that touch the checkboxes. 3.9 whenever the free plan interrupts - three times inside one form in 1h5z. then 3.12 and 3.13. IRZc runs 3.1 to 3.12 and ends on Discard with nothing saved.

questions.question: How often should this meeting repeat, and on which days?
questions.why: The custom recurrence dialog requires selecting a frequency interval and toggling the exact days of the week the meeting will take place.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to precisely tailor the meeting's recurring schedule to fit their personal or team availability.

questions.question: When should this recurring meeting series end?
questions.why: You must choose whether the series continues indefinitely, ends on a specific date, or stops after a set number of occurrences.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to align the meeting's lifespan perfectly with your real-world schedule or project duration.

children.label: Secure the meeting
children.note: Zoom only - Meet has no such section and Teams is never scheduled in the corpus. 3.7.1 then 3.7.2 then 3.7.3, in the order the form lists them; 3.7.4 is read and left off in every keeper. the corpus keeps the generated ID and the generated passcode every time and turns the waiting room on where it is off.

questions.question: Should you add guests to the event, or just make a link to share yourself?
questions.why: The event creation dialog provides options to "Add guests" for automated email invites or "Add Google Meet video conferencing" to generate and copy a link for manual sharing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent decides the method of distributing the meeting invitation to your intended participants.

questions.question: Is the Google Meet link actually on the saved calendar event?
questions.why: Checking the event details pop-up for the 'Join with Google Meet' button and link confirms that the meeting was properly generated for your invitees.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the reassurance of personally verifying that the correct video call link is attached to your specific calendar invitation.

questions.question: Does the meeting link in the event details match the one you originally generated?
questions.why: The meeting link shown for the birthday call at 08:00 is completely different from the link generated during the event creation at 11:05.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the guarantee that they and their invitees will actually end up in the same virtual meeting room.

children.label: Invite the participants
children.note: the invite is almost never sent inside the product. 4.1 or 4.2 on nearly every host - before the meeting from the saved details, or inside it from the Add others dialog or the Invite button. 4.3 on the two that edit what they copied. then 4.4 or 4.5 outside the product, where the corpus shows it at all. 4.6 from inside the meeting on Meet and Zoom. 4.7 on the Calendar and Teams routes, where the product sends. 4.8 on 6Yc8 and the .ics offers. 4.9 wherever a dial-in block is on screen. 4.10 on the two that switch to the recipient's inbox.

questions.question: How do you want to invite participants to the meeting?
questions.why: The dialog provides options to either copy the joining link to share manually or send an automated email invitation directly to specific contacts.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over the communication channel used to invite guests, as the agent might send an automated email instead of letting you share the link via your preferred messaging app.

children.label: Enter the meeting
children.note: guests run 5.1 to 5.7 - 5.1 always, 5.2 once, then one of 5.3 to 5.5, with 5.6 when the link did not carry the ID (6fIY) and 5.7 when there is no account (3Bje, 8bF-, QOUw). hosts of a scheduled meeting run 5.9; instant hosts arrive from 2. 5.8 on Zoom and Teams and Messenger - never on Meet. then 5.10 on every keeper that reaches the pre-join screen, then 5.11. 5.12 is where three guest joins end. 5.13 on the keepers that check what they are in - and in 8bF- guests cannot see the title before admission.

questions.question: Do the sender and the link in this email look like the meeting you expect?
questions.why: The email invitation provides both a prominent 'JOIN MEETING' button and a raw URL, requiring a choice of how to launch the call.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to visually verify the meeting's sender and URL details before launching the video call.

questions.question: Which scheduled meeting on your calendar do you want to join?
questions.why: The calendar displays multiple upcoming events like the 'Weekly check-in meeting' and 'Sales Team Meeting', so the exact meeting to attend must be identified.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide which specific meeting from your schedule to join at this moment.

questions.question: Do you want to join the Teams meeting from this email invitation?
questions.why: The email reading pane displays a 'Join' button for the weekly check-in Teams meeting, which is the direct path to entering the call.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to review the meeting's schedule and sender details before clicking the join link.

questions.question: Is the link in the browser exactly the one from the invitation?
questions.why: Pasting the URL directly into the browser's address bar is the most direct way to initiate the meeting platform's join flow.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify the exact meeting URL and choose which specific browser profile handles the link.

questions.question: Does the code typed into the join field match the one in the invitation exactly?
questions.why: The Google Meet homepage provides a specific text field to paste the code from your email, noting that dashes are optional.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the chance to verify the exact meeting code being used to access the call.

questions.question: Should the browser open the Teams desktop app?
questions.why: The browser prompt asks for permission to open the meeting in the Teams application, which determines whether the call takes place in the dedicated app or the web browser.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose between using the installed desktop application or continuing the meeting directly within the web browser.

questions.question: Should you download the desktop app or continue in the browser?
questions.why: The screen presents options to download the Teams app, open an existing app, or continue in the browser, which dictates whether new software must be installed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to choose whether to install a dedicated application on their device or proceed with the zero-installation browser route.

questions.question: Do you want to start the meeting from the card on the home screen?
questions.why: The screen displays your upcoming 'Private class with [name]' synced from Google Calendar, offering a convenient one-click shortcut to enter the call.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the contextual awareness of seeing their daily schedule and upcoming meetings laid out on the homepage before joining.

children.label: Set up audio and video
children.note: 5.10.1 on nearly every keeper - most demo a toggle and leave both on, and the teachers join with both off. 5.10.2 where the narrator checks devices - a settings pane in 2020, dropdowns under the buttons by 2024. 5.10.3 on Teams and 2021 Meet and in the meeting on the rest. 5.10.4 on every Zoom entry and where a phone option is read. 5.10.5 wherever the browser or the OS asks - product prompt first then browser prompt on Meet.

questions.question: How much noise suppression do you want on your mic?
questions.why: The audio settings pane lets you choose between Auto, High, Low, or Off to control whether background sounds like music or household noise are filtered out.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to tailor the noise cancellation level to your specific environment or current activity, such as playing music.

questions.question: Do you want to blur or replace your video background before joining?
questions.why: The pre-join screen provides a background settings pane where you can select a blur effect, choose a preset thumbnail, or upload a custom image to hide your real surroundings.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means you lose control over your personal privacy and how your environment is presented to other meeting participants.

questions.question: Which picture do you want as your background?
questions.why: The file explorer displays several image options like 'animated.jpg' and 'beach.jpg', and this selection determines the visual environment others will see behind you.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means losing the opportunity to curate the specific personal or professional aesthetic you want to present on the call.

questions.question: Should you allow the browser to access your camera and microphone?
questions.why: The browser requires explicit permission to use your camera and microphone so that other participants can see and hear you.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to trust this specific website with access to your computer's camera and microphone.

questions.question: Are you ready to join the meeting?
questions.why: The pre-join screen displays your active camera and microphone settings, serving as the final check before others can see and hear you.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally verify your camera feed, background, and audio setup before entering the shared meeting space.

questions.question: Do you want to join normally, or join already presenting your screen?
questions.why: The pre-join screen offers distinct 'Join now' and 'Present' buttons that determine how you initially interact with the meeting.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to enter as a standard participant with audio and video or to join strictly to share your screen.

questions.question: Does the meeting have any documents attached?
questions.why: The attachments tab indicates that any files added to the Google Calendar invite will be accessible here during the call.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to verify if any important reference materials were provided for the discussion.

children.label: Admit and manage the participants
children.note: host side only, entered when a guest asks to join. 6.1 as each guest arrives - 8bF- runs it twice by two routes. 6.2 before or after, where the waiting room was not set at scheduling. 6.3 whenever the host wants to see who is in. 6.4 to 6.7 as the tutorial bothers - and most of them are read out and not committed: the Mute and Remove dialogs in 0Qvm are never confirmed.

questions.question: Do you want to let this guest in? They aren't signed in.
questions.why: The screen warns that the person trying to join is not signed in to an account and might not be who they claim to be, requiring a choice to admit or deny entry.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means losing the ability to personally verify the identity of unknown participants before granting them access to the call.

questions.question: Who is in the meeting now, and has anyone joined or left?
questions.why: Checking the participants pane reveals exactly who is already in the meeting and who has not yet responded to their invitation.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the situational awareness of knowing which specific colleagues are present and who might need a reminder to join.

questions.question: Should you mute this participant for everyone on the call?
questions.why: The confirmation dialog warns that muting the participant will silence them for everyone and only they will be able to unmute themselves.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the contextual judgment of whether forcibly silencing a specific participant is appropriate for the current meeting dynamics.

questions.question: When removing a participant, do you want to block them or report them for abuse?
questions.why: The removal confirmation dialog includes checkboxes to fill out an abuse report or block the person from rejoining the call.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the discretion to decide whether a participant should just be temporarily removed for technical reasons or permanently blocked for inappropriate behavior.

children.label: Use the call controls
children.note: any order and any subset - this is the tour every keeper runs after 5.11. 7.1 and 7.2 nearly always; 7.3 and 7.5 where the narrator opens the menus; 7.6 on most; 7.7 and 7.4 where offered; 7.8 only on the Teams participant path; 7.9 once.

questions.question: After the mute, does the participant list actually show that person as muted, or is their audio still live?
questions.why: The screen shows the mute dialog opening, but after a cut, the participant list still displays an active audio icon instead of a muted one.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent would be confused by the inconsistent state and fail to learn how to properly complete the action.

questions.question: After the toggle, do the mic and camera buttons show the state you asked for?
questions.why: The screen displays toggle buttons for the camera and microphone, allowing you to control your privacy and background noise.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might leave your devices active by default, potentially broadcasting your private environment or background noise before you are ready.

questions.question: Do you want live captions on?
questions.why: The screen provides a 'Turn on captions' button that displays real-time text of the spoken conversation.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide if they need real-time visual text support to follow the meeting.

questions.question: How do you want to arrange the video feeds on your screen?
questions.why: The menu provides multiple layout options like 'Gallery at top' and 'Together mode' to customize how you view the other participants.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you lose the ability to choose a visual layout that best suits your personal viewing preferences for the meeting.

questions.question: Do you want to hide everyone's video and show only the shared content?
questions.why: Selecting 'Focus on content' from the 'More actions' menu removes the video gallery so the presentation can be viewed without visual distractions.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to customize your personal viewing layout to match your own focus preferences during the meeting.

questions.question: Do you want to pop out the shared content into a separate window?
questions.why: The top menu bar includes a 'Pop out' button that allows you to separate the presentation from the main meeting window to better manage your screen space.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you lose the ability to customize your personal screen layout and window arrangement during the live meeting.

questions.question: Do you want to pin your own share or camera to see what others see?
questions.why: Clicking the 'Presentation (You)' or 'You' thumbnails lets you enlarge your own feeds to confirm exactly what is being broadcast to the meeting.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the personal peace of mind that comes from visually confirming your camera and screen share look correct to others.

questions.question: What video resolution do you want to set for sending and receiving?
questions.why: The video settings offer high definition (720p) or standard definition (360p) options, allowing you to balance video quality against your available internet bandwidth.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might select a high resolution that causes lag on a poor connection, or default to a lower quality when you actually have the bandwidth for high definition.

questions.question: Does the call show a connection or quality warning?
questions.why: The Call health panel displays real-time technical metrics like the sent frame rate and latency to help you verify the quality of your connection.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally monitor the real-time technical quality of your connection and diagnose potential network or hardware issues.

questions.question: What message, emoji, or GIF should I send in the meeting chat?
questions.why: The screen shows the meeting chat pane with text input, emoji menus, and GIF search options for interacting with other participants.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally express their tone and spontaneous reactions using specific text, emojis, or GIFs.

questions.question: Which reaction do you want to put on the message?
questions.why: The screen shows a hover menu with multiple reaction icons like Heart and Laugh over the chat messages.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to express their personal emotional response to specific messages in the chat.

questions.question: Do you want to raise your hand or send a reaction?
questions.why: The Reactions menu displays emojis and a 'Raise hand' option that trigger visual feedback on your video feed to communicate silently with other participants.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally time your hand raise or select the most appropriate emotional reaction for the ongoing conversation.

questions.question: Do you want to open the queue for the raised hand?
questions.why: The screen displays a popup notification that a participant has raised their hand, offering a choice to either open the queue or dismiss the prompt.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to immediately acknowledge a participant's question or wait until a better time in the meeting.

questions.question: Do you want to take control of the shared presentation?
questions.why: The screen shows a shared presentation with a 'Take control' button and slide navigation controls.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent taking control without permission could disrupt the current presenter and the flow of the meeting.

questions.question: Should I open the slide grid so you can move through the slides on your own?
questions.why: The screen displays a grid view button that opens thumbnails of the slides, allowing you to jump to a specific slide on your end only.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to privately browse and review specific presentation slides at your own pace during the live meeting.

questions.question: Do you want to open the meeting notes panel?
questions.why: The in-call menu includes a 'Meeting notes' option to start capturing text notes directly within the meeting interface.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you lose the ability to personally format and record the initial discussion points for the team.

questions.question: Do you want to share the whole screen, a window, or a tab?
questions.why: The menu provides distinct sharing modes for your entire screen, a specific window, or a Chrome tab that is explicitly optimized for video and animation.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might not understand the specific media format or privacy requirements of your content to choose the most appropriate and secure sharing mode.

questions.why: The 'Edit your view' window provides a size slider and position icons so you can ensure your video feed doesn't block important shared content.

videoedit.task: edit a video in a video editor (CapCut, iMovie, DaVinci Resolve, Premiere, Clipchamp): import footage, make concrete edits — trim or split clips, add captions or text, add music or adjust audio, apply transitions or speed changes — and export the result; complete when the export finishes (the saved/share screen or the rendered file is shown). Surface pinned: the editing session itself — not editing-theory talks, not before/after showcases without the session. One-click AI editing flows (auto-edit, AI video generators like Sora or Runway) are off-task; ordinary tool features such as auto-captions used inside a manual edit are fine.

webdesign.task: design and publish a simple website in a site builder (Wix, Squarespace, Webflow, WordPress.com, Google Sites, Carrd): choose a template, edit pages and content (text, images, sections), configure the essentials (site name, domain path), and publish; complete when the published site's live URL is shown or visited. Surface pinned: the builder session — not web-design-theory videos, not code-from-scratch HTML/CSS courses. AI site builders (Wix ADI, 10Web, one-prompt site generators) are off-task: the arc must be manual template editing and publishing.

tree.label: Design and publish a website
tree.note: Start with 1 on every route that charges or offers a free tier, then 1.8 again whenever the user sees a payment or upgrade prompt later. 2 to get an account and reach the editor; the WordPress.org routes add 2.6 and 2.7. The user goes through 3 at different points depending on the route - at 1.7 for LMVE, WfqK and sx6l, at 2.1 for FFtR, at 9.6 for Gab9 and RAex, in settings for vBcs, after 9.7 for m9LG and S7S0, and after 9.4 for Tbal. then 4 to get a starting design; on the import routes 4.8 is the moment the site goes live. then the loop: for each page the user goes through 5 for its pages, menu and sections, and then 6 for the content of each section, with 7 whenever the change should show on every page and 9.2 or 9.3 whenever the user wants to see how the site looks - Tbal loops through five pages, Gab9 through four sections of one page. The user can go through 8 at any point, usually late in the task. 9 to publish, open the live site and check it, and 9.11 sends the user back into 5, 6 or 7. the task ends at 9.8.

children.label: Choose the builder and plan
children.note: Start with 1.1 in the recordings that show the user choosing a builder - in three of them the user follows an affiliate link or a recommendation, and in two the user searches. 1.2 wherever a free tier is on offer. then 1.3, and 1.4 to 1.7 only on the paid routes - LMVE, WfqK and sx6l at the start, Tbal at 9.4. 1.8 whenever the user sees a payment or upgrade prompt, at any point in the task. For example, the user meets two prompts in S7S0, leaves a checkout in vBcs, and closes a library prompt in LMVE.

questions.question: Does the layout hold together on mobile and tablet screens?
questions.why: Using the top bar device icons to preview tablet and mobile layouts ensures your content remains readable and properly aligned on smaller screens.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to visually verify and fine-tune the mobile viewing experience to match your personal aesthetic standards.

children.label: Set the site public or launch it

questions.question: Does the live address show the site, or a coming-soon page?
questions.why: Platforms like Squarespace or WordPress often default new sites to a private state or display a 'coming soon' splash page until a specific setting is toggled, even after clicking publish.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might share their new URL thinking the site is live, only to have visitors hit a password prompt or generic landing page.

questions.question: Ready to publish the site and make it public?
questions.why: Clicking the purple 'Go live' button commits your final edits and triggers the confirmation modal displaying your live URL.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the final opportunity to preview your work before officially launching the site to the public.

children.label: Read the publish confirmation and the URL

questions.question: What is the live address of the published site?
questions.why: The popup reveals the actual web address generated for your site, which might include unexpected numbers if your preferred name was taken, along with a button to check the live page.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to catch unwanted modifications to your free domain name and to personally verify that the live website looks correct.

questions.question: Was the live site opened from the confirmation page?
questions.why: The screen confirms the site is ready, making the view button the correct path to verify the published result.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user misses the opportunity to personally verify the live website and confirm the final URL.

questions.question: Does the live site reflect your latest edits, or is it displaying an older cached version?
questions.why: Site builders and browsers often cache pages aggressively. You might need to open an incognito window to verify that the latest published changes actually went live.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to confirm their final edits were successfully pushed to the public server, potentially leaving mistakes live.

children.label: Click through and read the live site

questions.question: Do the logo and menu buttons on the live site look like they did in the editor?
questions.why: Verifying the black outline on the [business name] logo and the pink navigation buttons ensures the site's visual branding matches your aesthetic vision before moving on.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to make subjective, fine-tuned aesthetic judgments like perfectly matching the navigation button colors to the logo's specific shade of pink.

questions.question: Do the prices and terms on the live page match what you gave?
questions.why: The screen displays specific pricing like $20 for a headshot and terms like extra characters costing 30%, which must be exact to set proper expectations with clients.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might use generic placeholder text or incorrect rates, losing the specific pricing and conditions you require for your commission work.

questions.question: What ads or 'made with' badges show on the live site?
questions.why: Identifying the persistent GoDaddy banners at the top and bottom of the page helps you evaluate if the free plan's forced branding is acceptable for your site's image.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you lose the opportunity to visually assess whether the platform's forced advertisements compromise the professional look of your finished website.

questions.question: Do the background or images need a last tweak after seeing the live site?
questions.why: The background color settings and image crop tool on the screen allow you to fix minor visual imperfections noticed during the live site review.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to apply your personal aesthetic judgment to subtle details like the exact background tint and image framing.

questions.question: Is any Lorem Ipsum or template placeholder text still on the live site?
questions.why: Templates are filled with dummy text to show layout. A sighted user scrolling the page will instantly spot Latin text or generic 'Write your description here' blocks, whereas an agent might only update the specific fields it was prompted to change.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user publishes a site that looks unfinished and unprofessional because leftover placeholder content was not visually identified and removed.
